claims.claim: By the best cell counts we have, a typical man is about half human.
claims.source_checked: Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016, PLoS Biol 14(8): e1002533, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002533, full text incl. Tables 1-3 and figure legends read in the PMC JATS XML (Europe PMC fullTextXML for PMC4991899); Hatton et al. 2023, 'The human cell count and size distribution', PNAS 120(39): e2303077120, doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120, full text read in the PMC JATS XML (Europe PMC fullTextXML for PMC10523466)
claims.note: Sender: 'We estimate the total number of bacteria in the 70 kg "reference man" to be 3.8·10^13 ... revise past estimates to 3.0·10^13 human cells'; 30/(30+38) = 44%. Hatton: '≈36 trillion cells in the male' (70 kg); with Sender's bacteria 36/74 = 49%. 44-49% is 'about half'. 'a typical man' = the 70 kg reference man both papers use; Sender's own summary calls this 'the typical adult human body'. Other Sender male groups: elder 22 vs 38 (37%), obese 40 vs 56 (42%), so 'typical' is doing necessary work and is accurate. 'Best cell counts' (plural) fair: Hatton calls Sender and Bianconi the 'Two important studies in the past decade', 'converging on values of 30 to 37 trillion human cells', and adds its own. 'Cell counts' excludes viruses, which are not cells; non-bacterial microbes are 2-3 orders fewer (Sender).

claims.claim: What a viewer who swipes at second two is left with: by t=2.0 s only 'By the best cell counts we have,' is spoken (alignment: 'have,' ends 1.96 s); Look 1 shows the dot figure with no text yet; Look 2 shows 'BY CELL COUNT' over the Vitruvian Man. Swiping at 3-4 s: 'a typical man is about half human' with 'ABOUT HALF HUMAN / typical 70 kg man, by count' (Look 1) or 'ABOUT HALF' + scrap 'TYPICAL 70 KG MAN' (Look 2).
claims.source_checked: Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016, PLoS Biol 14(8): e1002533, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002533, full text incl. Tables 1-3 and figure legends read in the PMC JATS XML (Europe PMC fullTextXML for PMC4991899); Hatton et al. 2023, 'The human cell count and size distribution', PNAS 120(39): e2303077120, doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120, full text read in the PMC JATS XML (Europe PMC fullTextXML for PMC10523466); src/generated/cell-count.alignment.json word timings; src/shorts/cell-count/index.tsx and src/shorts/cell-count-cutout/index.tsx (Tag/Word/Scrap timings)
claims.note: Nothing false is asserted before 2 s. The full hook names the body ('a typical man', spoken at 2.18-2.81 s, before 'about half' at 3.05 s) and the measure ('cell counts'), so the popular-but-wrong forms ('you are 10% human', 'you are half bacteria by weight', 'everyone is half bacteria') are not what a swiper takes away. The correction of the popular 10:1 is carried by the hook itself (Sender: 'This B/H value of about 1:1 ... should replace the 10:1 or 100:1 values'). In Look 2, 'ABOUT HALF' appears at F.less (3.05 s) and the 'TYPICAL 70 KG MAN' scrap at F.half (3.37 s); the man has already been spoken by then.

claims.note: Not supported by either source as a statement about the literature. Sender itself builds on the same authors' earlier estimate (ref 4, Sender, Fuchs & Milo, Cell 2016, 'Are We Really Vastly Outnumbered? Revisiting the Ratio of Bacterial to Host Cells in Humans') and a Microbe letter on the ratio (ref 5, Rosner 2014). True of the two counts cited: Hatton counts no bacteria and borrows Sender's ('with an approximately equal number of bacteria cells (17)'). Change: 'Of the two counts cited, the only one that pairs human cells and bacteria for the same reference body'.

claims.claim: 30 of 68 trillion is 44% human (Sender), 36 of 74 is 49% (Hatton with Sender's bacteria); Sender's reference woman is about a third human (21 and 44 trillion); its other groups 30-42%
claims.source_checked: Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016, PLoS Biol 14(8): e1002533, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002533, full text incl. Tables 1-3 and figure legends read in the PMC JATS XML (Europe PMC fullTextXML for PMC4991899); Hatton et al. 2023, 'The human cell count and size distribution', PNAS 120(39): e2303077120, doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120, full text read in the PMC JATS XML (Europe PMC fullTextXML for PMC10523466)
claims.note: Arithmetic checked: 30/68 = 44.1%, 36/74 = 48.6%. Sender Table 3: ref. woman 21 vs 44 (32%); young infant 1.9 vs 4.4 (30%); infant 4 vs 7 (36%); elder 22 vs 38 (37%); obese 40 vs 56 (42%).

claims.claim: Both papers count red blood cells as cells; against nucleated cells only bacteria outnumber them about 10:1 ('a question of definition'); microbial cells 'operationally' called bacteria; archaea and eukaryotes 2-3 orders of magnitude fewer
claims.source_checked: Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016, PLoS Biol 14(8): e1002533, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002533, full text incl. Tables 1-3 and figure legends read in the PMC JATS XML (Europe PMC fullTextXML for PMC4991899); Hatton et al. 2023, 'The human cell count and size distribution', PNAS 120(39): e2303077120, doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120, full text read in the PMC JATS XML (Europe PMC fullTextXML for PMC10523466)
claims.note: Sender: 'if one chooses to compare the number of bacteria ... to the number of nucleated human cells (≈0.3·10^13), the ratio will be about 10:1 ... seems to be a question of definition. We view red blood cells as bona fide cells'; 'Bacteria overwhelmingly outnumber eukaryotes and archaea in the human microbiome by 2–3 orders of magnitude [7,8]. We therefore sometimes operationally refer to the microbial cells in the human body as bacteria.' Hatton counts from 'the smallest red blood cells'.
